title: Power from the Tides
context:
A. Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the moon, with a smaller contribution from the sun, and in most coastal regions the sea rises and falls twice a day. This regularity gives tidal power a quality that few renewable sources can claim. Wind farms and solar panels depend on weather that can change within hours, whereas the timing and size of tides can be calculated for decades ahead with great accuracy. Engineers therefore regard tidal electricity as a dependable partner for more variable sources, even if it is unlikely ever to supply a whole nation on its own.

B. The oldest large tidal station still operating is on the Rance estuary in northern France, which opened in 1966. It works by trapping water behind a barrage, a wall built across the river mouth, and releasing it through turbines. The plant has produced electricity for more than fifty years, but its construction altered the estuary dramatically. Sand and mud now settle in different places, mudflats that once fed wading birds have changed, and fish migration has been disrupted. Such effects have made later proposals for barrages far more controversial than the French example once was.

C. A newer approach avoids walls altogether. Submerged turbines, resembling small wind turbines, are fixed to the seabed in channels where currents run fast. A pioneering array in the north of Scotland has fed power to the national grid since 2018. Because the blades turn slowly, usually only a few times a minute, studies using underwater cameras suggest that seals and fish tend to swim around them rather than being struck. Developers argue that this makes the technology gentler on wildlife than a barrage, although long-term monitoring is still in its early stages.

D. Money remains the biggest obstacle. Each unit of electricity from a tidal turbine currently costs several times more than the same amount from offshore wind. Equipment must survive in water that corrodes metal and constantly pushes against moving parts, so maintenance is demanding. Repair crews can only reach the machines during short periods of calm weather between tides, and a single failed bearing may take weeks to replace. These difficulties make private investors cautious, since they cannot be sure that the machines will last as long as the loans that paid for them.

E. Geography limits where tidal schemes can succeed. A difference of at least five metres between high and low water is generally needed to make a project worthwhile, and only a small share of the world's coastline meets that standard. The Bay of Fundy in Canada, the Severn Estuary in Britain and parts of the Korean peninsula are among the exceptional places. Even in these locations, the best sites are sometimes far from cities, so new power lines must be built to carry the electricity to the people who need it.

F. Researchers are exploring several ways to improve the economics. One idea is the tidal lagoon, an artificial ring of sea wall that encloses a shallow area and so affects a smaller stretch of coast than a river barrage. Another is to moor turbines beneath floating platforms that can be towed to shore for repair. Governments can also help by guaranteeing a fixed price for the electricity for many years, and some island communities have given residents a share of the income, which has increased local support for projects.
